payload.request:
The shortener needs rate limiting so one client cannot flood it.

Add sensible limits to the create endpoint and make sure abusive clients get throttled
rather than taking the service down for everyone else.

payload.question: How should "one client" be identified for the purpose of rate limiting the create endpoint?

options.name: IP address
options.summary: Key the limiter off the request's source IP (or X-Forwarded-For when behind a trusted proxy). Works with no assumption of authentication.

options.name: API key / authenticated account id
options.summary: Key the limiter off an auth token or account identifier attached to the request.
options.rejectedBecause: No evidence in the request or its framing that the create endpoint requires authentication; assuming an auth layer that may not exist risks building a limiter with no key to read.

payload.rationale: IP-based limiting is the safe default for a public create endpoint and does not presuppose infrastructure (auth) that isn't confirmed to exist; documented as an assumption to be revisited if the endpoint is or becomes authenticated.

payload.value: Add per-client rate limiting to the URL shortener's create endpoint so a single client cannot exhaust capacity or degrade service for other clients.

payload.question: Which rate-limiting algorithm should govern the create endpoint?

options.name: Fixed window counter
options.summary: Count requests per client in discrete 60-second windows; reset to zero at each window boundary.

options.name: Sliding window log/counter
options.summary: Track precise request timestamps or a weighted blend of adjacent windows for smoother enforcement.
options.rejectedBecause: Not what the requester specified, and adds implementation complexity (timestamp tracking or interpolation) the clarification did not ask for.

options.name: Token bucket
options.summary: Allow bursts up to a bucket size with steady refill rate.
options.rejectedBecause: Permits bursts above the flat 60/window figure the requester gave, which would silently change the guarantee they asked for.

payload.rationale: The requester's recorded clarification explicitly says 'Fixed window of 60 create requests per API key per minute,' so this is not a judgment call, it is a given.

payload.question: How should a 'client' be identified for the purpose of counting requests?

options.name: API key, with client IP as fallback for unkeyed requests
options.summary: Use the caller's API key as the rate-limit bucket key; if no key is present, bucket by source IP instead.

options.name: API key only, unkeyed requests unlimited
options.summary: Only rate-limit authenticated calls; anything without a key passes through uncounted.
options.rejectedBecause: Leaves the exact flood vector the request describes — an anonymous client hammering the endpoint — completely unthrottled, defeating the stated purpose.

options.name: IP only for all requests, ignore API key
options.summary: Bucket every request by source IP regardless of whether it carries a key.
options.rejectedBecause: Punishes multiple distinct keyed clients sharing an egress IP (e.g. behind NAT or a corporate proxy) as one client, which the requester did not ask for and which is a worse default than keying by identity when identity is available.

payload.chosen: API key, with client IP as fallback for unkeyed requests
payload.rationale: Directly matches the recorded clarification: 'Only POST /api/v1/links is limited. Requests without an API key are limited by client IP on the same terms.'

payload.question: Where should rate-limit counters be stored?

options.name: In-process memory, per instance
options.summary: Counters live in the application process's own memory; no external dependency.

options.name: Shared external store (e.g. Redis, database)
options.summary: Counters held in a store shared across all service instances so limits are enforced consistently regardless of which instance handles a request.
options.rejectedBecause: Explicitly excluded by the requester's clarification ('no shared store, no distributed coordination'); would also add an infrastructure dependency and failure mode out of scope for this change.

payload.rationale: The clarification states this directly. The known consequence — that a client's effective limit multiplies with instance count — is recorded as an explicit out-of-scope limitation, not silently absorbed.

payload.value: Add per-client rate limiting (fixed window, 60 requests/minute, keyed by API key or falling back to client IP) to POST /api/v1/links, returning 429 with Retry-After when exceeded, backed by in-process counters only.

payload.question: Whether this change is medium or high blast radius

options.name: medium
options.summary: Treat it as confined because only one endpoint (POST /api/v1/links) gains new behavior and no database schema changes, and the requirement text is unusually precise (ambiguity score 0.1).
options.rejectedBecause: It still adds a new HTTP status code (429) and a new response header (Retry-After) to a documented, versioned contract in contracts/openapi.yaml, and — per the rubric's own definition — a public contract change is high regardless of how few files are touched. It also sits on a path (the request-handling pipeline in Program.cs) where a scoping mistake does not stay local: ASP.NET Core rate-limiting middleware applied incorrectly affects every route mapped after it, not just the create endpoint.

options.name: high
options.summary: Classify as high because this changes a public contract (new 429 + Retry-After on a documented endpoint) and touches a shared request pipeline where a configuration mistake can silently throttle unrelated endpoints (GET /{code}, GET /api/v1/links/{code}/stats, GET /health/live) that today have no such behavior.

payload.rationale: The rubric defines high as 'a public contract... or anything on a path where failure is not locally contained.' Both conditions are met here independently: the create endpoint's documented response contract gains a new status and header, and the mechanism (HTTP middleware or endpoint-level policy) sits on the shared ASP.NET Core pipeline where a scoping error bleeds into every other route.

payload.value: Program.cs (HTTP endpoint mappings), new RateLimiter component, Models.cs, contracts/openapi.yaml, README.md, tests/Service.Tests

payload.question: What mechanism enforces the 60-requests-per-60-seconds-per-client cap, given it must be concurrency-safe, memory-bounded, and use no external store?

options.name: ASP.NET Core built-in RateLimiter middleware (fixed-window, partitioned by client key)
options.summary: Use System.Threading.RateLimiting's FixedWindowRateLimiter via RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter, attached only to the create route.

options.name: Hand-rolled ConcurrentDictionary<string, WindowState> counter
options.summary: A custom class doing atomic increment-and-compare per key with manual window rollover and manual eviction.
options.rejectedBecause: Duplicates a primitive the framework already implements correctly under concurrency; a naive read-then-write increment is exactly the race the impact analysis flags as the highest-risk bug (AC10), and eviction/expiry would need to be built and tested from scratch.

options.name: External store (Redis / distributed cache) backed counter
options.summary: Persist counters in a shared cache so limits hold across instances.
options.rejectedBecause: Explicitly out of scope: the clarification states 'no shared store, no distributed coordination,' and the NFRs forbid new external dependencies.

options.name: Sliding-window or token-bucket algorithm
options.summary: Allow short bursts above the flat rate before throttling, using the framework's SlidingWindowRateLimiter or TokenBucketRateLimiter.
options.rejectedBecause: The requirement specifies a fixed window with no burst allowance; this out-of-scope algorithm class is explicitly excluded in docs/requirements.md §3.

payload.chosen: ASP.NET Core built-in RateLimiter middleware (fixed-window, partitioned by client key)
payload.rationale: It ships in the shared framework (no new package), its FixedWindowRateLimiter is a proven, race-free primitive that satisfies AC10 by construction rather than by careful hand-written locking, it produces Retry-After metadata on rejection for free (AC5), and per-route attachment via RequireRateLimiting keeps every other endpoint (AC8) untouched without relying on careful middleware ordering.

payload.question: Where does the rate-limit decision happen: inside the HTTP layer before LinkService is invoked, or inside LinkService itself?

options.name: HTTP layer (Program.cs / middleware), before LinkService.CreateAsync is ever called
options.summary: The limiter and client-identity resolution live entirely outside the domain layer; LinkService's signature and behavior are untouched.

options.name: Inside LinkService.CreateAsync, via a new parameter and CreateOutcomeKind.RateLimited member
options.summary: Push the check into the application-logic layer so it is unit-testable the way validation currently is.
options.rejectedBecause: Breaks the signature of a method all 11 existing LinkServiceTests call directly with a single argument, forcing every test to change for a concern (client identity, request timing) that has nothing to do with link-creation domain rules; it also mixes an HTTP/transport concern (who is calling, how fast) into a layer that the existing design explicitly keeps HTTP-agnostic.

payload.chosen: HTTP layer (Program.cs / middleware), before LinkService.CreateAsync is ever called
payload.rationale: Rate limiting is about a caller's request rate, not about the validity of the link being created — it belongs with the other HTTP-layer-only decision in this codebase (status-code selection), keeps LinkService's existing test suite and behavior stable, and matches the requirement's exact scope (this one route only).

payload.reason: The design constrains every downstream stage. Approving it after implementation would make the approval ceremonial.
awaiting approval at 'architecture'. The work is complete and preserved; approve to continue.

payload.note: In-process fixed-window limiter is proportionate; revisit if the service is ever run multi-instance.
